name: Rear Naked Choke from Rear Triangle
description: Master the Rear Naked Choke from Rear Triangle position. Learn how triangle leg control frees both hands for the choke while eliminating common RNC defenses.
overview:
The Rear Naked Choke from Rear Triangle represents one of the highest-percentage finishing combinations in modern grappling. By establishing a triangle configuration with the legs around the opponent's neck and one trapped arm, the attacker creates a control framework that fundamentally changes the RNC dynamic. The triangle legs handle positional retention and limit the opponent's primary defense—two-handed grip fighting—because one arm is already trapped inside the leg structure. This frees both hands to work exclusively on establishing the choking grip.

Unlike the standard RNC from back control, where significant energy is spent managing hooks, maintaining the seatbelt, and fighting hand grips simultaneously, the rear triangle version separates these tasks between upper and lower body. The legs maintain control while the arms attack. This division of labor produces a significantly higher finishing rate and reduces the energy expenditure required to complete the submission. The trapped arm also acts as a wedge that enhances choking pressure on the carotid artery.

Strategically, this submission creates a cascading dilemma: defending the triangle squeeze exposes the neck to the RNC, while defending the RNC opens space for the triangle to finish directly. Skilled attackers cycle fluidly between these threats, making the combination extremely difficult to survive once fully established.

injury_risks.injury: Loss of consciousness from blood choke
injury_risks.recovery_time: Immediate to 30 seconds with proper release

injury_risks.injury: Trachea damage from improper forearm placement
Carotid artery injury from excessive force

safety_considerations.application_speed: SLOW and progressive - 3-5 seconds minimum in training. Never snap or jerk the choke. Partner should have full awareness of pressure building.
tap_signals: Verbal tap (say 'tap' or make any verbal sound)
Physical hand tap on opponent's body or mat
Going limp or loss of consciousness
Any distress signal or unusual sound
release_protocol: Immediately release choking arm upon tap signal
Remove hooks and body triangle if present
Gently guide partner to side-lying recovery position
Monitor consciousness and breathing for 30 seconds
If partner was unconscious, keep them lying down until fully alert
Never allow unconscious partner to stand immediately
training_restrictions: Never use competition speed or intensity in drilling
Never apply the choke to the trachea or windpipe
Always ensure partner has clear tap access with both hands
Stop immediately if partner makes any distress sound
Never hold a choke past the tap for any reason
Beginners must practice with extremely slow progression only

attacker.name: from Rear Triangle Attacker
attacker.description: Complete guide to finishing the Rear Naked Choke from Rear Triangle. Learn grip sequences, arm threading, and pressure application with triangle leg control.
attacker.overview: Attacking with the RNC from rear triangle is fundamentally different from a standard back control RNC because your legs are already doing the heavy positional work. The triangle configuration traps one of your opponent's arms inside the leg structure, which eliminates their most effective defense—the two-on-one grip fight. Both your hands are free to work the choking grip without competing for positional control. Your primary focus shifts from maintaining hooks and seatbelt to threading the choking arm deep under the chin and securing the figure-four grip behind the head. The triangle legs also create a squeezing pressure that compounds the RNC, making the finish come faster and with less energy than a traditional RNC.
key_principles: Use the triangle legs for all positional control so both arms can focus exclusively on establishing the choke
Thread the choking arm deep under the chin before attempting to close the grip—depth determines finishing power
Squeeze the triangle tighter when the opponent defends the RNC to create a compounding pressure dilemma
Keep your chest glued to the opponent's back throughout the finishing sequence to prevent rotation escapes
Control the opponent's free arm with your non-choking hand until the moment you lock the figure-four grip
Apply the choke by expanding your chest and pulling elbows together rather than cranking with arm strength
setup_requirements: Rear triangle position established with triangle legs locked around opponent's neck and one trapped arm
Chest-to-back connection maintained with hips angled toward the trapped arm side
Opponent's free arm controlled or at least monitored to prevent defensive gripping
Choking arm side clear of obstruction with space to thread forearm under the chin
Triangle lock tight enough that opponent cannot extract the trapped arm during the RNC attempt

execution_steps.description: Confirm your triangle lock is tight by squeezing knees together and pulling the locking ankle deep into the crook of your knee. Angle your hips toward the trapped arm side. Your opponent's one arm should be fully immobilized inside the triangle structure before you begin the RNC attack.

Use your non-choking hand to grab your opponent's free wrist or bicep. Pin it to their body or push it away from their neck to prevent them from establishing a defensive grip under their chin. This control window is critical—once you release it to lock the RNC, they cannot recover defensive grips.

Slide your choking forearm under the opponent's chin from the trapped-arm side. Drive your wrist bone across the throat line until your elbow is centered directly under their chin. The deeper you thread, the tighter the finish. Use a swimming motion if they tuck their chin—work the hand along the jawline until the forearm passes underneath.

Release the free-arm control and immediately place that hand on the back of the opponent's head or your own bicep. Lock the figure-four by gripping your choking arm's bicep with the supporting hand while the supporting hand presses behind the head. The blade of your forearm should sit across both carotid arteries.

Pull your elbows tight together while expanding your chest forward into the opponent's back. Angle your hips slightly to create a twisting pressure that enhances the carotid compression. The triangle legs should simultaneously squeeze tighter to compound the choking effect from the leg pressure with the arm pressure.

Finish the choke by driving your chest into their back while pulling elbows toward each other. Breathe out and expand your torso to increase pressure. Simultaneously tighten the triangle squeeze. The dual compression from arms and legs creates overwhelming pressure on both carotid arteries. Apply slowly in training and wait for the tap.

common_counters.counter: Opponent tucks chin tightly to block forearm from threading under
common_counters.your_response: Use a swimming motion along the jawline to work past the chin tuck. Alternatively, squeeze the triangle legs harder to create discomfort that forces them to address the leg choke, momentarily opening the chin defense.

common_counters.counter: Opponent uses free hand to grip and fight the choking wrist before it threads under the chin
common_counters.your_response: Strip the grip using your non-choking hand, then immediately re-thread the choking arm. If the grip fight persists, transition to attacking the free arm with a kimura or switch to finishing the triangle choke with legs only.

common_counters.counter: Opponent turns their body toward the choking arm side to relieve pressure and create space
common_counters.your_response: Follow the rotation with your hips and tighten the triangle squeeze to prevent further turning. Use the rotation to your advantage by extending your hips to finish the triangle choke directly rather than continuing the RNC.

common_counters.counter: Opponent bridges and attempts to roll over the non-choking shoulder to escape entirely
common_counters.your_response: Post with your free hand on the mat to maintain your base. Keep chest pressure on their back and ride the bridge. The triangle lock prevents meaningful positional change from a bridge because their arm and head are trapped in the leg structure.

common_errors.error: Releasing triangle leg pressure when transitioning to the arm choke
common_errors.consequence: Opponent extracts the trapped arm and recovers two-on-one grip defense, neutralizing the primary advantage of the rear triangle RNC
common_errors.correction: Maintain or increase triangle squeeze throughout the entire RNC finishing sequence—the legs handle control so the arms can attack

common_errors.error: Attempting to close the figure-four grip before threading the choking arm deep enough under the chin
common_errors.consequence: The choke lands on the jaw or forehead rather than the neck, creating a crank instead of a blood choke and giving the opponent time to defend
common_errors.correction: Prioritize forearm depth under the chin before worrying about locking the grip—thread until your elbow is centered under the chin

common_errors.error: Using arm strength to crank the choke rather than chest expansion and structural pressure
common_errors.consequence: Rapid forearm fatigue that causes you to lose the choke entirely, and the opponent can wait out the muscular effort
common_errors.correction: Finish by expanding your chest into their back and pulling elbows together using back muscles—let your skeletal structure do the work

common_errors.error: Neglecting to control the free arm before attempting to thread the choke
common_errors.consequence: Opponent establishes a two-on-one grip on your choking arm before it reaches the chin, stalling the attack indefinitely
common_errors.correction: Always pin or redirect the free arm with your non-choking hand before beginning the choking arm thread

common_errors.error: Losing chest-to-back connection by leaning away to create space for the choking arm
common_errors.consequence: Opponent uses the gap to rotate, flatten out, or begin escaping the rear triangle entirely
common_errors.correction: Keep your chest pressed into their back and use shoulder rotation rather than leaning to create the angle for threading the choking arm

common_errors.error: Placing the choking forearm across the trachea instead of across the carotid arteries
common_errors.consequence: Creates an airway choke that is slower, more painful, and risks trachea damage rather than a clean blood choke
common_errors.correction: Position the blade of the forearm laterally across the neck so it compresses both carotid arteries—the forearm bone should be on the side of the neck, not the front

training_progressions.focus: RNC grip placement and figure-four locking from rear triangle
training_progressions.description: Drill the choking arm thread and figure-four lock with a compliant partner already in rear triangle bottom. Focus on forearm depth, proper blade-of-forearm placement on the carotids, and smooth grip closure. No resistance. 20 repetitions per side.

training_progressions.focus: Maintaining triangle pressure while establishing the RNC
training_progressions.description: Partner holds rear triangle bottom while you practice the full sequence: tighten triangle, control free arm, thread choke, lock grip, finish. Partner provides light resistance on the free arm and chin tuck. Focus on not losing triangle tightness during the arm attack.

training_progressions.focus: Adapting to defensive reactions during the finishing sequence
training_progressions.description: Partner actively defends with chin tucks, grip fights on the choking wrist, and rotation attempts. Practice stripping grips, swimming past the chin, and transitioning between triangle choke and RNC threats based on what the defense presents.

training_progressions.focus: Finishing under full resistance in positional sparring
training_progressions.description: Start in rear triangle top with partner at full resistance. 3-minute rounds with the goal of finishing the RNC or any submission from the position. Track finishing rate and identify which defensive patterns give you the most trouble for targeted drilling.

knowledge_assessment.question: What anatomical structures does the Rear Naked Choke from Rear Triangle primarily attack?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The RNC attacks both carotid arteries simultaneously. The blade of the choking forearm compresses one carotid while the bicep of the choking arm compresses the other. The supporting hand behind the head prevents the opponent from pulling away. The triangle legs add additional compression on the carotid from the trapped-arm side, creating a three-point pressure system that produces rapid blood flow restriction to the brain.

knowledge_assessment.question: Why does the rear triangle configuration make the RNC significantly more effective than from standard back control?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The triangle legs trap one of the opponent's arms inside the leg structure, eliminating their most effective defense—the two-on-one grip fight where both hands work together to strip the choking arm. With one arm immobilized, the defender has only one free hand to fight two attacking arms. Additionally, the triangle legs handle all positional control, freeing both of the attacker's hands to work exclusively on establishing and finishing the choke.

knowledge_assessment.question: Your opponent has their chin tucked tightly and you cannot thread your forearm underneath—what are your two best options?
knowledge_assessment.answer: First, use a swimming motion where you work your hand along the jawline from one side, using your fingers to walk past the chin before turning the wrist to seat the forearm. Second, squeeze the triangle legs harder to create a compounding leg choke that forces the opponent to address the leg threat, which typically lifts the chin enough to thread the forearm underneath. Alternate between these approaches to create a rhythm that overwhelms the chin defense.

knowledge_assessment.question: What is the correct forearm placement to ensure a blood choke rather than an airway choke?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The blade of the forearm (the bony edge of the radius) must sit laterally across the neck, compressing the carotid arteries on each side. The forearm should NOT press directly on the front of the throat or trachea. Thread the arm deep enough that the elbow sits centered under the chin, placing the forearm and bicep on opposite sides of the neck. If you feel cartilage or the opponent coughs, adjust laterally until you are on soft tissue over the arteries.

knowledge_assessment.question: Your opponent is grip-fighting your choking wrist with their free hand—how do you break through this defense?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Use your non-choking hand to strip their grip by peeling fingers or redirecting their wrist away from the defensive position. Once cleared, immediately re-thread the choking arm before they re-establish the grip. If the grip fight is persistent, use the triangle leg squeeze to create pain and urgency that distracts from the grip defense. You can also switch to attacking the free arm itself with a kimura threat, which forces them to release your choking wrist to defend the shoulder lock.

knowledge_assessment.question: What should you do immediately if your training partner goes limp during the choke application?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Immediately release all choking pressure from both the arms and the triangle legs. Gently guide your partner to a side-lying recovery position. Do NOT allow them to sit up or stand. Monitor their breathing and consciousness. Most practitioners regain consciousness within 5-20 seconds. If they do not wake within 30 seconds or have irregular breathing, call for medical assistance. Stay calm, keep them lying down, and reassure them when they wake.

knowledge_assessment.question: How does the dual compression from triangle legs and choking arms compound the finishing pressure?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The triangle legs compress the carotid artery on the trapped-arm side from a posterior angle while the choking forearm and bicep compress both carotids from an anterior angle. This creates three distinct pressure vectors converging on the blood supply to the brain rather than the typical two from a standard RNC. The result is faster onset of blood restriction and a shorter window for the opponent to escape. The defender must address both pressure sources simultaneously, which is significantly more difficult than defending a single choking mechanism.

knowledge_assessment.question: What are the key indicators that the choke is properly set and will produce a finish?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The forearm blade sits laterally across one carotid with the bicep pressing the other, the elbow is centered under the chin, and the figure-four is locked behind the head. The opponent's defensive movements weaken or become erratic, and you feel their body relax slightly. In training, a properly set blood choke produces a tap within 3-8 seconds of full application. If you have been squeezing for more than 10 seconds without a tap, the placement is likely off—release, adjust, and re-apply rather than adding more force.

knowledge_assessment.question: When should you abandon the RNC attempt and switch to an alternative submission from rear triangle?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Abandon the RNC if the opponent has established a strong grip defense that you cannot strip after two clear attempts, if you are losing triangle tightness while fighting for the choke, or if the opponent is successfully creating rotation away from the choking arm. In these cases, transition to the triangle choke finish by squeezing legs and angling hips, attack the trapped arm with an armbar by extending hips, or switch to a bow and arrow grip if wearing the gi. The rear triangle supports multiple submissions—never force a single finish at the cost of the position.

knowledge_assessment.question: What is the proper speed and progression for applying this choke in training versus competition?
knowledge_assessment.answer: In training, apply the choke slowly over 3-5 seconds minimum, allowing your partner to feel the pressure build and tap before any risk of unconsciousness. Never snap or jerk into the finish. In competition, the choke can be applied more quickly once the grip is locked, but the initial arm threading should still be controlled to ensure proper carotid placement. The rear triangle variant finishes faster than standard RNC due to compounding pressure, so extra caution in training is warranted because the margin between a secured choke and unconsciousness is shorter.

defender.name: from Rear Triangle Defender
defender.description: Complete defense guide against Rear Naked Choke from Rear Triangle. Learn to recognize the threat, protect the neck, fight grips, and escape to safety.
defender.overview: Defending the RNC from rear triangle is among the most challenging defensive scenarios in grappling because you are fighting a two-layer attack simultaneously. Your opponent's triangle legs control your posture, trap one arm, and compress your neck from behind, while their freed hands attack your neck with the RNC. Unlike defending a standard RNC where you can use both hands for grip fighting, you have only one free hand available because the other is immobilized inside the triangle structure. Your survival depends on recognizing the threat early, protecting the neck before the choking arm threads underneath your chin, and systematically working to either prevent the figure-four lock or escape the rear triangle position entirely. Timing is critical—once the RNC grip is fully locked from this position, the compounding pressure from legs and arms makes escape nearly impossible.
key_principles: Protect the neck immediately by tucking your chin to your chest and bringing your free hand to your collar line before the choking arm threads under
Address the choking arm first—preventing the forearm from passing under your chin is the highest priority defensive action
Use your free hand for two-on-one grip defense on the choking wrist whenever possible to stall the arm thread
Work to extract the trapped arm from the triangle to restore full defensive capacity before the choke is locked
Create rotation toward the non-choking side to reduce the angle of the RNC and buy time for escape
Manage breathing deliberately through the nose to conserve energy under restricted airflow
recognition_cues: Opponent releases seatbelt or free-arm control and begins swimming one hand toward your chin or neck from behind
You feel the opponent's triangle legs tighten simultaneously as their upper body shifts to thread the choking arm
Opponent's non-choking hand pins or redirects your free arm away from your neck, clearing the path for the choke
You feel wrist or forearm pressure along your jawline as the opponent attempts to work past your chin tuck

defensive_options.action: Two-on-one grip defense on the choking wrist using your free hand and the trapped arm's hand if accessible
defensive_options.when_to_use: As soon as you feel the opponent's arm beginning to thread toward your chin—this is the earliest and most effective intervention point
defensive_options.if_successful: Stalls the RNC attack and forces the opponent to spend energy on grip stripping, buying time for escape
defensive_options.risk: If the opponent strips your grip, you may be worse off because you spent energy fighting the arm rather than escaping the triangle

defensive_options.action: Chin tuck with shoulder shrug to create a physical barrier against the forearm threading under the chin
defensive_options.when_to_use: When you feel the opponent's hand approaching your neck and you cannot establish a grip on their wrist in time
defensive_options.if_successful: Prevents the choke from being set and forces the opponent to use swimming or jawline pressure to bypass your defense
defensive_options.risk: A determined attacker can eventually work past the chin tuck, especially with the triangle adding compounding pressure

defensive_options.action: Rotate body toward the non-choking arm side while fighting the triangle legs to disrupt the finishing angle
defensive_options.when_to_use: When the opponent has begun threading the choking arm but has not yet locked the figure-four grip
defensive_options.if_successful: Disrupts the RNC angle and may create enough space to begin escaping the rear triangle entirely
defensive_options.risk: Rotation can expose your back further if not combined with active hand fighting, and the opponent may follow the rotation

defensive_options.action: Extract the trapped arm from inside the triangle to restore full defensive capability
defensive_options.when_to_use: Whenever you can create any space in the triangle—ideally before the opponent begins the RNC attack but viable throughout
defensive_options.if_successful: Restores both hands for grip fighting and significantly reduces the choking pressure from the triangle legs
defensive_options.risk: The extraction attempt may temporarily reduce your neck defense as you redirect focus to the arm

escape_paths: Strip the choking grip and extract the trapped arm to transition back to standard back control defense
Rotate toward the non-choking side and use frames to recover Closed Guard or Turtle position
Create enough space to pull the head through the triangle opening and recover to Turtle

favorable_outcomes.how: Successfully rotate toward the non-choking arm side while fighting the triangle structure, then use frames and hip movement to slide into the opponent's closed guard where you can begin a guard passing sequence

Prevent the RNC from being locked by maintaining chin tuck and grip fighting on the choking wrist, stalling the attack until the opponent abandons the RNC attempt and you remain in the rear triangle position where other escape opportunities exist

common_errors.error: Focusing entirely on fighting the choking arm while ignoring the triangle leg pressure compounding the choke
common_errors.consequence: Even if you successfully fight the RNC arm, the triangle legs continue compressing the carotid arteries, and you may lose consciousness from the leg choke alone
common_errors.correction: Address both threats simultaneously—fight the choking arm with your free hand while using your trapped arm and body positioning to relieve triangle leg pressure

common_errors.error: Pulling the choking arm away from the neck rather than pinning it close to prevent further threading
common_errors.consequence: Pulling creates space that the attacker uses to adjust angle and re-thread deeper, actually accelerating the choke setup
common_errors.correction: Pin the choking wrist tight against your collarbone or chest using a C-grip—keep it close rather than pushing it away

common_errors.error: Panicking and making explosive escape attempts that burn energy without technical purpose
common_errors.consequence: Rapid exhaustion under restricted blood flow leads to faster loss of consciousness and eliminates the window for a methodical escape
common_errors.correction: Stay calm, breathe through the nose, and execute small deliberate movements—each defensive action should have a specific technical goal

common_errors.error: Waiting too long to tap when the choke is fully locked and escape is no longer viable
common_errors.consequence: Loss of consciousness, potential injury from uncontrolled collapse, and unnecessary risk in a training environment
common_errors.correction: Recognize when the figure-four is locked with proper forearm placement and tap immediately—there is a 3-5 second window between a locked choke and unconsciousness from this position

knowledge_assessment.question: What is the earliest moment you can recognize the RNC attack from rear triangle and what should your immediate response be?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The earliest recognition point is when the opponent releases their control on your free arm or seatbelt grip and begins swimming their hand toward your chin line. Your immediate response is to tuck your chin firmly to your chest, shrug your shoulders up, and bring your free hand to your collarbone ready to intercept the choking wrist. Acting in this early window is the difference between a stalled attack and a locked choke.

knowledge_assessment.question: When should you tap to the Rear Naked Choke from Rear Triangle to avoid injury?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Tap immediately when you feel the figure-four grip lock behind your head with the forearm properly seated under your chin across the carotid arteries. From this position with the triangle adding compression, you have approximately 3-5 seconds before loss of consciousness. Do not wait to feel dizzy or see spots—these are signs that unconsciousness is imminent. Tap early and often in training. There is no benefit to holding out once the choke is structurally complete.

knowledge_assessment.question: Why is extracting the trapped arm from the triangle the most important long-term defensive goal?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The trapped arm is what makes the entire attack system work. It prevents you from using both hands for grip defense against the RNC, it acts as a wedge that increases carotid pressure from the triangle legs, and it limits your ability to create rotation or frames for escape. Once the arm is extracted, you restore full defensive capacity with both hands, the triangle loses its structural choke, and you can defend the position like standard back control where escape rates are significantly higher.

knowledge_assessment.question: What defensive adjustments should you make if the opponent begins squeezing the triangle legs harder while setting up the RNC?
knowledge_assessment.answer: When the triangle squeeze intensifies, immediately grip the opponent's top leg at the ankle or behind the knee with your free hand to resist further tightening. Turn your chin toward the non-choking side and press your trapped arm's elbow against the inner thigh of the bottom triangle leg to create a wedge. Use short controlled breaths through your nose to manage the restricted blood flow. These combined actions prevent the triangle from finishing on its own and maintain enough defensive structure to fight the incoming RNC.

training_progressions.focus: Identifying the RNC setup cues from rear triangle bottom
training_progressions.description: Partner establishes rear triangle and cycles through RNC setup movements at slow speed. Defender practices recognizing each cue—arm release, hand swim, wrist approach—and executing the chin tuck and hand-to-collar response. No finishing. Build pattern recognition over 20+ repetitions.

training_progressions.focus: Two-on-one and single-hand grip defense against the choking arm
training_progressions.description: Partner attempts to thread the choking arm at moderate speed while defender practices C-grip on the wrist, pinning the arm to the collarbone, and stripping grips. Partner resets and tries again from different angles. Focus on keeping the defensive hand close to the neck rather than reaching away.

training_progressions.focus: Combining RNC defense with rear triangle escape sequences
training_progressions.description: Partner applies RNC from rear triangle at 60-70% intensity. Defender must defend the choke while simultaneously working arm extraction and positional escape. Practice transitioning from grip defense to active escape without abandoning neck protection during the transition.

training_progressions.focus: Defending and escaping under competition-level pressure
training_progressions.description: Positional sparring starting in rear triangle bottom with partner attacking the RNC at full intensity. Defender earns points for preventing the choke for 60 seconds, additional points for escaping the position entirely. Build the composure and technical precision needed for real defensive scenarios.
